To eulogize someone means to speak or write about them with deep, heartfelt, and very high praise — publicly, and in a formal or serious way.

When you eulogize someone, you are not just saying "they were great." You are delivering a tribute — a thoughtful, glowing, often emotional expression of admiration — usually in front of an audience.

The word "eulogize" is most strongly associated with funerals and memorial services. When someone dies, a friend, family member, or colleague often stands up and delivers a speech that honors the person's life — their character, achievements, kindness, and impact. That act of delivering such a speech is called eulogizing.

"The priest eulogized the man as a devoted father and a pillar of his community."

"She eulogized her best friend at the funeral, sharing stories that made the audience both laugh and cry."

So in this most common use, to eulogize someone is to honor a person who has passed away through words of the highest praise, delivered to others who are also mourning.
But It Is Not Only Used for the Dead

While funerals are the primary setting, "eulogize" can also be used when someone living is being honored in a deep and formal way — such as at a retirement ceremony, a lifetime achievement award, or a tribute event.

"At the gala, the director's colleagues eulogized him for his forty years of groundbreaking work."

"The documentary eulogizes a living legend who transformed modern music."

In these cases, the person being eulogized is still alive, but the level of praise is so deep, warm, and formal that the word still fits perfectly.
What Makes It Different from Just "Praising"

This is a very important distinction.

You praise your friend for cooking a delicious meal. You compliment your colleague on a good presentation. But these are casual, everyday expressions of approval.

To eulogize is entirely different. It implies:

  • The praise is deep and serious, not casual
  • It is expressed publicly — in front of an audience, or in writing meant to be read by others
  • The tone is solemn, warm, and reverential — almost sacred
  • The subject is being honored in a lasting and meaningful way

Think of it this way: eulogizing is praise turned up to its most serious, formal, and heartfelt form.

When someone eulogizes another person, they do not list their flaws or give a balanced review. A eulogy is entirely celebratory and admiring. The speaker focuses on the best of who that person was — their virtues, their contributions, the love they gave, the lives they touched.

This is why the word carries a sense of reverence — a deep respect, almost like you are treating the person as something precious and worth honoring.
It Can Also Be Used for Things, Not Just People

Less commonly, you can eulogize an idea, an era, an institution, or a place — essentially anything that deserves a tribute.

"The writer eulogized the dying art of handwritten letters in her final essay."

"His memoir eulogizes a lost way of life in rural India."

Here, the writer is giving a sorrowful, loving tribute to something disappearing or already gone.
A Subtle Nuance: When the Praise Feels Excessive

Sometimes writers use "eulogize" with a slightly critical edge — to suggest that the praise being given is too early, too much, or undeserved.

"The press was already eulogizing the young athlete as the greatest of all time, and he had only played three professional games."

This use implies: the praise is so grand and so final that it feels premature or overdone. This is a more sophisticated, literary use of the word, but good to be aware of.

These all come from the same family and will help you fully own the word:

  • Eulogy (noun) — The actual speech or written piece of tribute. "She delivered a beautiful eulogy."
  • Eulogist (noun) — The person who delivers the eulogy. "The eulogist spoke for twenty minutes."
  • Eulogistic (adjective) — Describing something full of high praise. "The review was entirely eulogistic."

To eulogize someone is to:

  • Praise them deeply and formally, in words
  • Usually publicly — in a speech or written piece
  • Most often after their death, but also to honor the living
  • With a tone that is warm, serious, and full of admiration
  • In a way that celebrates the very best of who they are or were

It is the most solemn and heartfelt form of praise there is — the kind of words you would want spoken about you when you are no longer here.
